quick: Rabbit ATG 1.5 mg/kg/day IV; equine ATG 10-15 mg/kg/day IV (regimen-specific)
Use only if clearly needed; potential fetal harm
Discontinue nursing or drug; excretion unknown
summary: Antithymocyte immunoglobulin (ATG) is a polyclonal antibody preparation (rabbit- or equine-derived) that depletes circulating T lymphocytes, used to treat or prevent organ transplant rejection and to treat aplastic anemia. Infusion-related cytokine release and profound immunosuppression with infection risk are the principal hazards; premedication and slow infusion are required.
indications: Treatment of acute organ (especially renal) transplant rejection
Prophylaxis of acute rejection / induction immunosuppression in solid organ transplantation
Treatment of acute aplastic anemia (often with ciclosporin)
Prevention/treatment of graft-versus-host disease and conditioning in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (per protocol)

dosage.d: 1.5 mg/kg/day IV over >=4-6 h for 7-14 days
10-15 mg/kg/day IV for 14 days, then alternate-day to day 21
1-1.5 mg/kg/day IV for several days perioperatively

admin: Administer by slow intravenous infusion through a high-flow vein or central line over at least 4-6 hours
Premedicate with corticosteroid, antihistamine and antipyretic to reduce cytokine release reactions
Use an in-line filter; do not exceed recommended infusion concentration
Have resuscitation equipment available; slow or stop infusion for reactions
Adjust or withhold dose for leukopenia or thrombocytopenia per protocol
moa: Polyclonal immunoglobulins bind multiple surface antigens on human T lymphocytes, causing complement-dependent lysis and opsonization/clearance of T cells from the circulation and lymphoid tissue. The resulting T-cell depletion and functional modulation suppress cell-mediated immune responses, reducing graft rejection and autoimmune marrow destruction.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to rabbit or equine proteins / the specific product
Active acute or chronic infection that contraindicates further immunosuppression
relative: History of severe systemic reaction to prior ATG

preg: Animal data and class effects suggest potential fetal harm; use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether ATG is excreted in human milk; because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the infant, discontinue nursing or the drug.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for renal impairment, but monitor closely; renal transplant recipients are the common population.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; monitor liver enzymes and overall tolerability during therapy.

major: Other immunosuppressants (calcineurin inhibitors, corticosteroids, mycophenolate) - additive over-immunosuppression and infection/malignancy risk
Live attenuated vaccines - avoid; risk of disseminated infection
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant during acute parenteral therapy.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and may interfere with serologic/cross-match testing.

monitoring: Complete blood count with platelets daily during dosing
Vital signs continuously during infusion for cytokine release reactions
Signs and symptoms of infection (including CMV/EBV) during and after therapy
Renal and hepatic function and graft function as appropriate
counsel: This medicine strongly suppresses your immune system - report any fever, chills, sore throat or signs of infection promptly
Infusion reactions (fever, rash, breathing difficulty) may occur and will be monitored
Serum sickness (joint pain, rash, fever) can appear days after treatment
Avoid live vaccines and contact with people who have infections
Long-term, there is a small increased risk of certain cancers
pk: Rapid T-cell depletion within hours of infusion
Serum levels peak at end of infusion
Rabbit ATG approximately 2-3 days (range up to ~30 days)
T-cell depletion may persist for weeks to months
Refrigerate 2-8 C; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Rabbit ATG (thymoglobulin) is more potent and dosed lower (~1.5 mg/kg) than equine ATG (~10-20 mg/kg)
Premedication and slow infusion markedly reduce cytokine release reactions
Profound, prolonged immunosuppression raises risk of opportunistic infection (CMV) and PTLD
Dose is commonly titrated to peripheral T-cell or absolute lymphocyte count
missed: Doses are given in a supervised inpatient/transplant setting on a defined schedule; a delayed or missed dose is managed by the transplant team per protocol, not self-administered.
overdose: No specific antidote. Excessive dosing increases risk of profound leukopenia/thrombocytopenia and infection; manage with supportive care, dose interruption, growth factors/transfusions and aggressive infection surveillance.
